n: Once Israel has taken over the Canaanite cities and homes, they must build a justice system that protects innocent life.
Three cities west of the Jordan were to be set apart as places of refuge. Moses had already named three east of the Jordan.
Roads were to be prepared and the land divided into thirds, so no one would be too far from safety.

f.g: Build and maintain roads to the cities.

n: These cities were for someone who killed another person accidentally, with no prior hatred.
A classic example: two men chopping wood, and an axe head flies off its handle and kills one of them. That person may flee and live.
Without refuge, a grieving relative seeking vengeance might catch and kill the innocent person in the heat of anger.

f.g: Hebrew go’el — the nearest kinsman responsible for avenging a family member’s death.

n: So the command is repeated: set apart three cities.
If God expands Israel’s territory as he promised the patriarchs…
…and if Israel stays faithful, three more refuge cities should be added for the larger land.

f.g: There is no clear record this was ever done.

n: The purpose: no innocent blood should be shed, bringing guilt on the whole land.

f.g: Bloodguilt would rest on the nation.

n: Refuge did not protect murderers — those who hated their victim, ambushed them, and killed deliberately.
The murderer’s home-town elders would bring him back from the refuge city and hand him over to justice.
No misplaced pity for a murderer. Purging the guilt of innocent blood protects the nation’s well-being.

f.w: put away the guilt of innocent blood

n: Moving a boundary stone was a way of secretly stealing land. Ancient family boundaries were sacred inheritance from God.

f.g: A boundary marker, usually a stone.

n: A basic principle of justice: no conviction on one witness. Two or three must agree. This law of witnesses runs through all of scripture.

f.w: at the mouth of two witnesses, or at the mouth of three witnesses

n: What if a witness lies to harm someone?
Both parties appear at the sanctuary before priests and judges — that is, before the Lord.
The judges investigate carefully to uncover the lie.
The liar receives the very penalty he tried to bring on the innocent person. Lies meant to destroy turn back on the liar.

f.w: as he had thought to have done unto his brother

n: Such justice would deter others from bearing false witness.
The “law of retaliation” set punishment equal to the harm — no more, no less. It limited revenge; Jesus later taught a higher law of turning the other cheek.

f.w: eye for eye, tooth for tooth
